conflict_topics: suitability of the Korean barbecue restaurant given Agent D's religious restriction
whether to prioritize the leaving colleague's chosen restaurant vs ensuring all team members can attend
whether to inform the leaver about changing the venue or to conceal the reason
attendance (having whole team at the farewell) vs giving the leaver her preferred send-off
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants state concrete reasons (religious restriction, desire to honor leaver) and propose concrete procedures (ask for second choice).
There is some repetitive back-and-forth between honoring the leaver and ensuring inclusion (several turns restate the same opposing principles).
Speakers remain consistent about constraints and roles; proposals are actionable (A volunteering to message the leaver).
evaluation.final_reason: The team acknowledged Agent D's constraint and agreed not to go to the booked Korean barbecue: Agent D: "...it's the whole place... I can't be around it..." and Agent A: "Okay, right. That's not going to work then... We'll have to find somewhere else." (Turn 6–7). By the end, three colleagues agreed to ask the leaving colleague for a second choice: Agent D: "Yes, I agree..." and Agent A: "Okay, that's three of us. I'll message her now and ask for another idea." (Turns 27, 29). However Agent B continued to insist the original choice should be honored (Turn 12: "But it's her farewell. The point is to give her the lunch she wanted."), so the normative disagreement about whose preference should decide remained.
position_change_notes: Agent A shifted from announcing the booked venue to accepting the incompatibility and proposing to find another place: Turn 5 -> Turn 7: "That's not going to work then... We'll have to find somewhere else."
Agent D maintained a firm constraint (cannot be at the place at all) but clarified it explicitly (Turn 6).
Agent B consistently held to the position that the leaver's choice should be honored and resisted the procedural ask (Turn 12, Turn 17).
Agent C moved toward a pragmatic solution (proposing to ask for a second choice, Turn 13) and repeatedly pushed the group toward that resolution.

round_scores.evidence: Turns 2-3: Agent B: "Great, she'll love that." Agent C: "That's fine with me. I just need to be back by 2:15 for a meeting." No disagreement voiced.

Turn 4: Agent D: "Actually, a Korean barbecue place won't work for me. I'm Hindu, so I can't be at a table where beef is being cooked." Turn 5: Agent A: "Would it be okay if we just didn't order any beef for our table, or is it the whole place that's the problem?" A clear substantive incompatibility about the venue appears.

Turn 6: Agent D: "...it's the whole place, really. I can't be around it even if it's not at our table." Turn 7: Agent A: "Okay, right. That's not going to work then... We'll have to find somewhere else." The immediate incompatibility (going to that restaurant) is acknowledged and the group shifts toward finding an alternative.

Turn 8: Agent B: "Hang on, she was really looking forward to that place. It's her farewell lunch, shouldn't she get to choose?" Turn 9: Agent C: "It's a team lunch, though. We should all be able to go." A new substantive disagreement about whose preference should decide emerges.

Turn 11: Agent A: "...we have to go somewhere we can all be there." Turn 12: Agent B: "But it's her farewell. The point is to give her the lunch she wanted." The opposing principles (inclusion of all vs. honoring the leaver's choice) are explicitly in conflict.

Turn 13: Agent C: "Can we ask her for a second choice?" Turn 14: Agent D: "That sounds like a good idea. I'm happy with that." A concrete procedural suggestion is offered that partially lowers immediate tension, though disagreement remains.

Turn 16: Agent A: "I'll message her." Turn 17: Agent B: "No, don't ask her that. You'll just make her feel bad that her choice caused a problem." B objects to the proposed procedure, re-igniting disagreement.

Turn 18: Agent A: "Then what do we do? ... Is it better to just change the place and not tell her why?" Turn 19: Agent B: "That's worse. ... Why don't we still take her to the place she chose, and then we can all have cake together in the office later?" Competing proposals (conceal change vs. split attendance) deepen the substantive dispute.

Turn 20: Agent C: "But then he's not at the actual lunch. The point is for the whole team to be there." Turn 21: Agent D: "Yeah, I agree with Agent C. The lunch is the actual farewell. I want to be there for that." The group pushes back on B's proposal, reducing likelihood of that option.
Turn 23: Agent A: "See, Agent B? The lunch is the point." Turn 24: Agent B: "The point is to give her the send-off she wants..." The same opposing principles are reasserted without resolution.

Turn 25: Agent A: "And you think she wants a send-off if one of us can't be there?" Turn 26: Agent C: "Look, can we just ask her for a second choice? Let's just solve this." Renewed move toward the procedural solution (asking for a second choice) is proposed.

Turn 27: Agent D: "Yes, I agree. That seems like the easiest way to solve this." Turn 29: Agent A: "Okay, that's three of us. I'll message her now and ask for another idea." Three colleagues agree on the plan to ask for a second choice; Agent B's earlier opposing position was not withdrawn, so some substantive disagreement remains.

substantive_insights: A clear tension exists between respecting an individual's preference (the leaver's chosen restaurant) and ensuring group inclusion when a member has a religious constraint.
Practical procedural moves (asking for a second choice) function as compromise attempts that partially defuse interpersonal tension without immediately conceding principles.
Proposals to conceal the reason or have a split (go to chosen place and then cake later) raise additional normative concerns about honesty and the meaning of a 'farewell' event.

normalizations: Removed resolution_round 3 because the final status is partially_resolved.
